desc:
Count the rectangular blocks of the grid matrix that contain exactly area cells and whose cell sum is at most limit.

A block is a set of consecutive rows and consecutive columns. A block of height h and width w has area h * w; shapes h x w and w x h are different shapes (if h != w), and blocks at different positions are counted separately.

matrix = [[1, 2, 3],
          [4, 5, 6]], area = 2, limit = 5
1 x 2 blocks with sum ≤ 5: [1, 2] = 3, [2, 3] = 5
2 x 1 blocks with sum ≤ 5: [1, 4] = 5
result = 3
hints: Only shapes h x w with h * w = area matter. How many such shapes can there be?
The number of divisors of area is small (at most a few dozen), and each shape must also fit inside the grid.
For every valid shape, slide it over all positions and read each block sum from a 2-D prefix table in O(1). Count the positions with sum ≤ limit.
editorial: List the shapes: every divisor h of area with h ≤ R and area / h ≤ C gives one shape (h, area / h). Since the heights differ, no shape is counted twice (a square shape appears once).

Build the usual 2-D prefix table P. For a shape (h, w) every top-left corner (i, j) with i + h ≤ R and j + w ≤ C gives a block sum P[i+h][j+w] - P[i][j+w] - P[i+h][j] + P[i][j]. Count those that do not exceed limit.

A grid has at most 3,600 positions and an integer up to 3,600 has at most 60 divisors, but only divisors that fit in the grid matter, so the work is O(R * C * d) with a small d. Without the prefix table each block would cost area extra steps.
